stated_availability: No formal data availability statement appears anywhere in the article (the back matter runs CRediT authorship contribution statement -> Declaration of competing interest -> Acknowledgements -> Appendix A -> References). The only availability statements are: (1) Methods 2.3.3, "All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0. The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information."; (2) Methods 2.4, "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information."; (3) Appendix A. Supplementary data, "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921." Underlying record-level morphometric datasets are attributed to prior publications, two unpublished PhD theses (Martin-Ramos 2022; Key 2015), two monographs (Petrie 2020; Robb 2007), and author-curated replica assemblages, with no stated deposit or accession. DESCRIPTIVE ONLY - not mapped to L1-L6 (L-levels are assigned at reproduction time from actual retrieval attempts, preregistration section 7.3).

F1.evidence: No dataset-level persistent identifier. The only PID in the paper is the article DOI (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921), which identifies the article, not the data; Appendix A points to that same article DOI for 'Supplementary data'. No Zenodo/Dryad/figshare DOI, no repository accession, no tDAR/Open Context identifier, no IGSN for the measured artefact assemblages. Per the FAIR guide F1 test, resources reachable only via a container URL/DOI without their own PID score 0.

F2.evidence: No structured dataset metadata record exists. The supplement is described only as 'Supplementary data to this article' (Appendix A); supplementary items are referred to by bare labels ('Supplementary Tables 1 and 2', 'Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2') with no creator/title/keyword/description metadata, no data dictionary and no codebook. Rich structured metadata (authors, title, keywords, abstract) exists only at article level, not for the data resource.

F3.evidence: No dataset metadata record exists in which an identifier could be embedded (F2 = 0). There is no landing page, DataCite/Crossref dataset record, or README carrying a data PID; the DOI printed in Appendix A is the article's own identifier.

F4.evidence: The data are not registered or indexed in any searchable data registry. No deposit in Zenodo, figshare, Dryad, DataCite-indexed repository, or the domain repositories relevant to archaeology (tDAR, Open Context, ARIADNEplus). Discoverability is limited to the publisher's article page carrying an undifferentiated supplement.

A1.evidence: A1 completeness rule applied: data_completeness.coverage_category is 'minimal' (0 of 18 enumerated datasets accessible at Tier 0-2), so A1 = 0 per the instrument. The full research dataset (~5,000 morphometric records across 18 assemblages) is dispersed across prior publications, two unpublished PhD theses ('Martin-Ramos, C., 2022 ... Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London'; 'Key, A.J.M., 2015 ... Unpublished PhD Thesis, University of Kent'), two monographs (Petrie 2020; Robb 2007), and author-curated replica assemblages ('the specimens have since been curated at the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory'), with no retrieval route stated. The ethical-restriction exception does not apply: no ethical, legal, or CARE-based restriction is claimed anywhere in the paper.

A1_1.evidence: Assessed for the accessible portion per the FAIR guide. The retrievable material (Appendix A supplementary data, including the results tables and figures) is delivered over HTTPS from the publisher platform at no cost and without login, the article being gold open access: '0305-4403/(c) 2023 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).' HTTPS/DOI resolution is an open, free, universally implementable protocol.

A1_2.evidence: The retrieval protocol (HTTPS via the publisher platform and DOI resolver) supports authentication/authorisation where required, and none is required here - the accessible portion is openly licensed with no gating. Nothing is 'completely closed with no justification' within the accessible portion; no ethical or CARE-based restriction is invoked (none applies to metric data on lithic, ceramic, and metal artefacts).

A2.evidence: Metadata describing the datasets persist independently of the supplementary files: the article is Crossref-registered under DOI 10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921, is open access under CC BY, and itself documents each dataset (sample sizes, variables, units, sites, chronology, curation location, measurement protocols) in Sections 2.3.1-2.4.4 and Tables 1, 5-7. If the supplementary files were withdrawn, this publisher-committed, permanently archived description would remain retrievable - unlike a personal website or unarchived repository.

I1.evidence: No formal, machine-actionable knowledge representation is evidenced for the data. No file formats are stated for the supplement; the data as presented in the article are PDF tables (Tables 1, 5-7) of descriptive statistics and range values, which the FAIR guide explicitly classes as available but not machine-actionable ('Data in PDF supplementary materials is available but not machine-actionable'). No CSV-with-schema, JSON, XML, or self-describing format is documented.

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabulary, ontology, or thesaurus with PIDs is used. Artefact typologies ('Thebes cluster' style, Clovis/Folsom/Midland, 'Impressed Ware' and 'Stentinello' styles) and chronological terms (MIS 15, Howiesons Poort, Early Archaic) are given as free text with bibliographic citations only - no Getty AAT, PeriodO, Pleiades, CIDOC-CRM, or ARIADNEplus terms or URIs anywhere in the paper.

I3.evidence: No qualified, typed references with PIDs link the data to other resources. Upstream data sources are given as author-date citations only, e.g. 'Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study of scaling laws in Paleoindian points' and 'The methods used to collect these data have been previously described in Martin-Ramos (2022)'; the reference list is almost entirely DOI-free (one DOI appears, for Key and Gowlett 2022). No 'is derived from [DOI]' style relationship typing exists.

R1.evidence: The data are richly described in the article with a plurality of relevant attributes: each of the 18 assemblages is documented with site, region, chronology, sample size, measured variables and units, and measurement protocol (e.g. 'we limit the present case study to the whole flakes excavated from MIS 15 sediments in the 2020 season (n = 173)'; 'We use length (mm), breadth (mm), thickness (mm) and mass (g) data recorded from each core following the method outlined by de la Pena and Wadley (2014)'), plus descriptive statistics in Table 1 and per-variable ranges in Tables 5-7, including explicit handling of duplicates and missing estimates ('Na' indicates that estimates were not able to be returned using the OLE method).

R1_1.evidence: A clear, machine-readable licence covers the article and its Appendix A supplementary data: '0305-4403/(c) 2023 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (SPDX: CC-BY-4.0, with resolvable licence URL). No separate or conflicting data licence is stated.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance is documented for the data: creation process and sources ('500 replica Acheulean handaxes were produced by Key and Lycett (2017) on British flint over the course of 18 months'; 'originally knapped by M.I.E. in 2021 with the intention of conducting a ballistics experiment'), excavation and curation context ('Roughly 500 flint handaxes were excavated from low energy fluvial contexts'; 'curated at the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory'), transformations (duplicate removal and the resampling procedure of Section 2.4.1.6.1), and funding/collection credit in the Acknowledgements ('Collection of capuchin flake data was made possible by a British Academy Fellowship'; 'Excavations to collect the Old Park flake data were funded by a Leakey Foundation Grant to AK').

R1_3.evidence: No domain-relevant community data or metadata standard is applied. There is no Dublin Core, DataCite, Darwin Core, CIDOC-CRM, or ARIADNEplus conformance, and no deposit under a discipline repository's standards (tDAR, Open Context). Measurement protocols are standardised against prior papers (e.g. 'recorded in mm following Buchanan and Hamilton (2021)'; 'according to the procedure described in Cortell-Nicolau (2019)'), which is methodological consistency rather than a community data/metadata standard as required by R1.3.

F1.evidence: No software persistent identifier. The scripts are stated to sit in the publisher supplement only - 'The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.3.3) and 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.4) - with no Zenodo software DOI, no SWHID, no CRAN package, and no repository release. The article DOI in Appendix A identifies the article, not the code.

F2.evidence: No structured software metadata: no CodeMeta.json, no CITATION.cff, no repository landing page with creator/title/version fields. The code is referred to only as 'the script', with no name, version, author attribution at artefact level, dependency list, or description beyond its purpose.

F3.evidence: No software metadata record exists that could carry a code identifier (F2 = 0); there is no landing page, DataCite/Software Heritage record, or CITATION.cff embedding a PID for the scripts.

F4.evidence: The code is not registered or indexed in any searchable software registry - no Zenodo, Software Heritage, CRAN, JOSS, or institutional software catalogue entry. It is discoverable only as an undifferentiated attachment to the article page.

A1.evidence: The code is stated to be retrievable via a standard protocol: the two R scripts are published as part of Appendix A supplementary data, reachable over HTTPS from the open-access article ('Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921'), not by email or personal request. Scope is stated to be complete for the analyses ('all validation analyses'; 'all case study tests'). The data-completeness cross-reference in the instrument applies to data FAIR only, so it does not zero this cell; note the supplement itself was deliberately withheld from this assessment, so retrieval rests on the authors' statements.

A1_1.evidence: Delivery is by open, free, universally implementable protocol: HTTPS/DOI resolution from the publisher platform, with the article gold open access under CC BY ('This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)'), so no subscription, login, or proprietary client is needed to obtain the supplementary scripts.

A1_2.evidence: The HTTPS/DOI retrieval route supports authentication and authorisation procedures where necessary, and none is necessary here: the scripts are openly published with no access gating and no restriction claimed. Nothing about the code is closed without justification.

A2.evidence: Descriptive metadata for the code persist independently of the files themselves: the Crossref-registered, permanently archived open-access article records the code's existence, purpose, and runtime ('All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0. The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information'), plus authorship of the analysis through the CRediT statement (Key: 'Formal analysis'; Jaric: 'Formal analysis, Methodology'). This survives any withdrawal of the supplementary files.

I1.evidence: The code uses a formal, accessible, shared representation: plain-text R scripts in a widely implemented open-source language, with the interpreter version pinned - 'All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0' (Section 2.3.3). Per the FAIR guide, standard-format source code (Python/R) earns I1.

I2.evidence: No FAIR vocabularies or controlled terms are applied to the software. No CodeMeta/SPDX-based metadata vocabulary, no ontology terms, and no named R packages or namespace declarations are given; the OLE method is referenced only through the literature ('The formulaic expression of OLE is widely available through open-access sources (e.g., Pimiento and Clements, 2014; Roberts et al., 2021; Key et al., 2021b))'.

I3.evidence: The code carries no qualified, typed references with PIDs to related resources: no declared dependencies with versions or DOIs, no 'uses software [DOI]' or 'is supplement to [DOI]' relationships. Links to prior methods and data exist only as author-date citations in the article prose.

R1.evidence: The code artefact itself is not richly described. Its entire documentation in the paper is two one-line mentions ('The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information'; 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information'); no README, usage instructions, input/output specification, function documentation, or installation guidance is described or claimed.

R1_1.evidence: The scripts are published as part of Appendix A of an article released under a clear, machine-readable licence: 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (SPDX: CC-BY-4.0). Clear and accessible, though CC BY is a content rather than a software licence and no code-specific licence (MIT/GPL/Apache) is supplied.

R1_2.evidence: No provenance metadata attach to the code: no version number, no version-control history or release, no dependency/package versions, and no random seeds despite heavily stochastic procedures ('One thousand iterations of each process were performed for all subsampling percentages and k'; 'We repeated the OLE procedure with randomised values for 1000 iterations'). Only the R interpreter version (4.3.0) and CRediT roles are recorded, which falls short of documented creation process for the artefact.

R1_3.evidence: No community software standards are met: the code is not packaged to CRAN/rOpenSci standards, has no CITATION.cff or CodeMeta.json, no tests, no environment specification (no renv.lock, requirements file, or container), and no archived release. It sits at Level 1 of the computational reproducibility spectrum (code only, no dependency or environment specification).

barriers: No data availability statement in the article; the only stated supplementary contents are the two analysis scripts, not the underlying morphometric records

Unpublished PhD theses as data sources: Olduvai Bed III-IV cleavers (n = 134) from 'Martin-Ramos, C., 2022. Acheulean Technology and Hominin Cognition ... Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London'; eight further Acheulean handaxe assemblages from 'Key, A.J.M., 2015. Form and Function in the Lower Palaeolithic. Unpublished PhD Thesis, University of Kent'

Closed monographs as data sources: Middle Historic ceramic bowls (n up to 1466) recorded 'see: Petrie, 2020' (Oxbow Books); Neolithic Impressed Ware and Stentinello pots 'following Robb (2007)' (Cambridge University Press)

Author/co-author held material with no deposit: replica handaxe assemblage (n = 500, produced by Key and Lycett 2017) and replica Early Archaic points (n = 45), whose 'specimens have since been curated at the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory'; only descriptive statistics are published (Table 1)

Record-level data for the remaining case studies (Old Park flakes n = 173; Boxgrove handaxes n = 254; Sibudu bipolar cores n = 131; Paleoindian Clovis n = 810, Eastern Clovis n = 228, Folsom n = 179, Midland n = 64; geometric microliths phase A n = 344 and phase B n = 390; capuchin flakes n = 31; copper socketed tang points n = 93) are cited to prior publications (e.g. 'Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study') with no repository, accession, or supplement pointer given in this paper

Data presented in this article are PDF tables of descriptive statistics and OLE range estimates (Tables 1, 5-7) rather than the ~5,000 record-level measurements the OLE models consume, so in-article extraction cannot substitute for the source datasets

Verification limit: the publisher supplement was deliberately withheld from this assessment, so tiering follows the paper's own statements and content; no upstream source could be checked for embedded data (no web access)
